passage:
Monday. Parul and Harish were playing carrom on the veranda when Harish said her striker had touched the line, so she must give up the queen. "It did not touch," said Parul. "It did," said Harish. Both folded their arms and the game stopped.

Wednesday. The same fight started again. This time Parul said, "Here is what I saw. Now you tell me what you saw." Harish told her. Neither changed their mind, so Parul suggested asking Harish's cousin to watch.

Saturday. The cousin sat between them and called every close shot the same way for both. They agreed on a new rule: a striker on the line loses the turn. The game lasted all afternoon.

qa.q: Where were Parul and Harish playing carrom?
qa.a: They were playing on the veranda.

qa.q: How was Parul feeling when she said, "Now you tell me what you saw"?
qa.a: She was probably tired of the same stuck fight and wanted to settle it fairly, so she asked to hear Harish's side instead of repeating her own.

qa.q: What could the two of them do if the cousin is not around next time?
qa.a: They could write the line rule down together before starting, or ask another fair person to watch the close shots.

qa.q: How might Harish see Parul's idea of asking Harish's cousin?
qa.a: Harish may have felt relieved that someone neutral could decide, though Harish might also have worried the cousin would rule against Harish.

grounding: Two friends both claim to be right in a carrom dispute; one states her view, hears the other and they bring in a fair referee and agree a rule.
